title: Prayer of the Guest Chaplain of the U.S. Senate: Rabbi Dr. Joshua Loth Liebman on 19 May 1948

coauthors.name: Joshua Loth Liebman
coauthors.bio: Joshua Loth Liebman (1907–1948), born in Hamilton, Ohio, was a Reform movement rabbi in the United States and best-selling author, best known for hia self-help book Peace of Mind (1946), which spent more than a year at #1 on the New York Times Best Seller list. Liebman graduated from the University of Cincinnati in 1926 after which he was ordained and earned a doctorate from Hebrew Union College. From 1934 to 1939, Liebman served as rabbi of K.A.M. Temple (Chicago, Illinois). In 1939, Liebman became the rabbi of Temple Israel (Boston, Massachusetts). In September 1947, the rabbi and his wife Fan took in a teenager, Leila Bornstein, a Polish-born survivor of the Auschwitz concentration camp.

coauthors.bio: The Congressional Record is the official record of the proceedings and debates of the United States Congress, published by the United States Government Printing Office and issued when Congress is in session. Indexes are issued approximately every two weeks. At the end of a session of Congress, the daily editions are compiled in bound volumes constituting the permanent edition. content:
Guest Chaplain: Dr. Joshua Loth Liebman, rabbi, Temple Israel, Boston, Massachusetts
Sponsor: n/a
Date of Prayer: 19 May 1948

Contribute a translation Source (English)
O God, Father of all men,
we thank Thee
for this great Senate of democracy
in this hallowed America.
Cause us to understand
that laws are given
that men shall live by them[1] Leviticus 18:5 
and not die by them.[2] Yoma 85b.3 
Inspire these lawgivers
to make America an ever more beautiful gem of earth
where cooperation shall be the dream
and equal justice the dynamic goal—
America thus the example to all the world.
Cause us to realize
that now all nations,
from the oldest unto the newest, Israel,[3] The Israeli Declaration of Independence was announced only five days prior, on 14 May 1948. 
dwell today on the same street of atomic destiny,
and therefore we must live and work together
so that our children’s children
shall have a planet to inherit.
God,
enable these architects of law
to build the wider mansion of human welfare—
Thy kingdom on earth
where all Thy children shall live together
“for the blessing of all
and the hurt of none,
for the joy of all
and the woe of none.”[4] A quotable phrase from an address offered before Hadassah on 25 October 1947 by Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver (head of the American section of the Jewish Agency for Palestine and chairman of the American Zionist Emergency Council). “A positive decision at the United Nations will be a victory for the United States and for the Soviet Union… These two great powers have been brought together on the Palestine issue while they fail to see eye to eye on almost every other issue. For the Jewish people, an affirmative decision will mean the beginning of a new epoch in history. The manner in which the Arab peoples react to the decision of the United Nations will also have great consequences for them. It may mean prolonged and costly conflict which will benefit no one, or it may mean cooperating for the regeneration of the entire Near East for the blessing of all and the hurt of none.” 
Amen.

This prayer of the guest chaplain was offered in the fifth month of the second session of the 80th US Senate, and published in the Congressional Record, vol. 94 part 5 (19 May 1948), pp. 6051-6052.
